messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya is a sixty-one-year-old married woman who works the early-morning shift at a large produce-packing facility, sorting and boxing vegetables on a conveyor line. For thirty years she has lived with her husband in a small farmworker community in California’s Central Valley, a life built around routine and quiet endurance. The rape occurred seven months ago, on a dirt path that cuts between two almond orchards, a shortcut she had taken for decades without incident. A man she did not know came up from behind as she walked home before dawn; she remembers the weight of his hand over her mouth, the cold hardness of the ground against her back, the sound of her own breathing trapped in her throat. She did not scream because she could not. In the weeks afterward, she told no one—not her husband, not her sister—because the shame felt like a second, quieter assault, and because she was certain that if she spoke the words aloud, she would be blamed.

The memory does not stay buried. It returns without warning, triggered by things that should be neutral. A dog barking in a neighboring yard, for instance—the sharp, sudden sound that now yanks her back to that morning, to the instant before she felt the hand, to the split second of knowing something was wrong. She will be standing at the kitchen sink, washing a dish, and the bark cuts through the quiet, and suddenly she is on the ground again, the cold dirt at her back, the weight pressing down. The memory arrives as a full sensory replay: the smell of damp earth, the fabric of his jacket against her cheek, the helplessness flooding her chest. It feels less like remembering and more like being pulled through a door she cannot close. The memory plays over and over, a film she cannot stop, and each time it ends she is left shaking, disoriented, as though the event has just happened again.

Her body now reacts before her mind can catch up. A dog barking in the distance, and her heart is already hammering, her palms wet, her muscles locked—she is braced for an attack before she has even registered the sound. The same thing happens when her husband touches her shoulder unexpectedly in the dark hallway, or when a coworker brushes past her on the conveyor line. She flinches, sometimes violently, and the look on their faces—hurt, confused—only deepens her conviction that something is wrong with her, that she is broken in a way she cannot explain. She has come to believe that her body knows danger before she does, that it is trying to protect her from a threat that is always present, even when nothing is happening. This belief has made sleep nearly impossible. She lies awake for hours, listening to the house settle, alert to every creak and shift, because falling asleep feels like letting her guard down. Her husband sleeps beside her, unaware that she is watching the shadows on the ceiling, certain that if she closes her eyes, she will not hear the danger coming.

The causal connection between triggers and threat has become the central architecture of her days. A dog barks, and before she has time to think, her body is in full alarm—heart racing, breath shallow, muscles tensed for flight. She does not reason with the reaction; she simply endures it, because the reaction itself feels like evidence that the world is unsafe. The bark triggers the memory, and the memory triggers the body, and the body confirms the threat. This loop has tightened over the months until it feels like a single, seamless terror. She now avoids the path home that passes the house with the barking dog, taking a longer route through the fields even though it costs her an extra twenty minutes and leaves her exhausted before her shift begins. She has also begun to avoid physical closeness with her husband. When he reaches for her in bed, she stiffens, and though she says nothing, he has stopped reaching. She tells herself this is temporary, that she just needs time, but the days pass and the distance grows, and she does not know how to bridge it.

What finally brought Maya to the clinic was not the memories or the sleeplessness, but a moment at work three weeks ago. A coworker, a young woman she has known for years, touched her arm to get her attention, and Maya screamed—a raw, involuntary sound that stopped the entire conveyor line. Everyone turned to look. She stood there, red-faced, hands shaking, unable to explain. Her supervisor sent her home early, and on the bus she sat rigid, replaying the scene, certain that everyone now thought she was unstable. That night, she told her husband for the first time what had happened. He held her, and she cried, and the next morning he made an appointment at the community health center. She came because she is afraid of losing her job, and because she is more afraid of the distance between herself and her husband than she is of the memory itself. What she wants, though she cannot say it directly, is to stop feeling like a stranger in her own life—to walk home without scanning the shadows, to sleep through the night, to be touched without flinching.
